description.text: Silvia, also known as Sylvia, lived in the late fifth and early sixth centuries (c. 515 – c. 592).  She was the mother of Pope Gregory the Great and came from a distinguished Roman family; her husband, Gordianus, was a regionarius of the gens Anicia.  Her native place is sometimes cited as Sicily and sometimes as Rome, and the family home was located on the Clivus Scauri.

After Gordianus died around 573, Silvia devoted herself to religious life in a new cell by the gate of Blessed Paul.  She continued to support Gregory’s monastic house by providing vegetables from her garden, and a mosaic portrait of her parents was later executed at the monastery of Saint Andrew.  Early veneration of Silvia is evident: she built a chapel on the Aventine, was honoured by Romans as a Christian widow, and later monks from Mar Saba settled in her house, dedicating it to Saint Sabas.

curiosities.text: Silvia is venerated as a patroness of pregnant women, and she is invoked by expectant mothers for a safe delivery.
She provided fresh vegetables from her garden to support the monastic community founded by her son Gregory, demonstrating her practical piety.
A mosaic portrait of Silvia and her husband was commissioned by Gregory the Great and is described in detail by Johannes Diaconus at the monastery of Saint Andrew.
